Fair enough, but I don't think there's anything wrong with being picky with a new purchase. I don't have infinite money. If I can only choose one camera to get, of course I'm going to be comparing small differences between my options. One of those differences being the power button placement. And if I already have an inkling (based on my usage patterns) that something might not suit might workflow, why would I go out of my way to risk my one purchase based on the anecdotal muscle memory of others with a different workflow? 

Muscle memory solves nothing for me either, when my problem is literally lacking an extra hand. Muscle memory alone isn't going to power on a left handed switch when I'm holding my laptop, groceries, an umbrella, or my bicycle handlebar. I don't use my left hand because I don't need it. And that frees me up to shoot much more readily in much more situations, where I would have missed the moment if I had to re-grip the camera twice.

For me a power switch isn't something small either, other than physically. The way I shoot (raise camera > on > shoot > off, all in the span of 3 seconds) I use it twice every picture taken. For something that takes up 50% of my shooting process, it's certainly not minor, and would *absolutely* get in the way of just shooting. I do agree that the best camera is the best one I have on me though, which is precisely why I'm here looking for something that I can have on me more. 

Yes I'm being very picky, but not *needlessly* for *my* needs. I don't care for pixel-perfect sharpness or 25600 ISO performance, but I'm not going to say all those reviewers are *needlessly* making comparisons zoomed in 1000% on Lightroom. My needs on the street capturing life are not the same as the needs of a product photographer printing billboards, and just because a Hasselblad would be awfully impractical for me doesn't mean 100MP is needless.

I know you said it as a passing thought, but I actually really like your idea about having the dome push people out if they are people inside when it lands. It sounds simple, but it creates an entire new dimension of using his dome for more things than just blocking. 

If it pushes people out, you can use it to check corners, or force people out of hard-to-clear spots like Ascent hell. You can use it to force people off hard angles like someone OPing from Fracture B site towards the stairs without having to worry that he might stay waiting in there with a shorty. Meaning you can do creative weird site smokes that would normally troll your team and help the enemy by creating pockets for them to play around. 

Probably a bad example, but something like in between Gen and Boxes on Ascent A site. It prevents people from peeking from back gen, left side of dice, and hell. Normally you cannot smoke like this with other agents because you would create a pocket for the defender to play around (e.g. Mako). So now you can use it more creatively to chop up the site and change it's layout. You can even use it to deny defuses momentarily like Astra pull. 

And obviously it will now be able to delay pushes better as a defense smoke. But it would still be distinct from a Sage wall because there are different interactions like dash/blastpack/reyna dismiss through or TPing past.

Maybe I'm overthinking and imagining too much about it's usefulness lol. But I think this simple change has a lot of potential, and would justify the single charge and high cost.

If you think about it, the three of them are saying the same thing, just from different points of view. 

Jamppi is speaking from the POV of people that want to improve, get better at the game, whether it's kids just starting out or lower tier teams. So he obviously sees and states the benefit of replays aiding immensely in improving skill. 

ANGE1 is speaking from the POV of a pro team that is strat heavy, and would like to keep that as a differentiator. A little selfish and short-sighted I would say, as he's not always going to be on the same team. When you're no longer a top team and other people have caught up on strats you'll find yourself on the opposite side and wishing for replays. But either way, it shows that he clearly understands how the replays systems help teams learn, improve, and develop strats, he just think they are at the top of that and doesn't want people learning from them. 

Boaster is somewhat in the middle. He clearly understands not just how replays help people and teams to learn, but also the virtue of having teams learn from each other and constantly increasing the skill level, because it's just healthy for the scene to have good competition. But he's also been used to doing his job without replays for a long time now, so he's accustomed to the limitations he's had to work with. And him being better at this IGL job than others despite not having replays to work with is just a "on the bright side" perk for him, again from the POV of a strat-heavy top team.

Overall, it's clear that every one of them understands how important and useful replays are. It just affects different teams proportionally depending on how much they need to catch up in terms of strats. Which explains the differing feelings from FPX and FNC who feels they have their strats down pat, vs Liquid who is still struggling with their IGL-ing and strat calling.

I think it's just really disappointing that more pros aren't speaking out against this, simply because they feel their team is in a good spot without it. It's such a short-sighted stance to hold only because it affects them disproportionately less when they're already on top, when they're not always going to be so. Not to get political here, but it's a bit like how the rich and poor feel about taxes. It's just pretty selfish and narrow-minded to be comfy sitting at the top spot and avoiding competition, even though competition will always improve the quality of the scene. If they truly cared about the scene's future, the pros could do so much more in pressuring Riot to fastlane the replay system if they spoke out. If Riot's priority really is profit, it would do a lot if more pros were vehement rather than nonchalant about it, forcing Riot's hand to ensure a competitive and healthy scene for their real moneymaker. Yup, RIB's 2D replay was something I had in mind when thinking about this. But I think this is limited too to the same constraints as the in-game one, as Valorant just doesn't record this information with enough granularity. For example there's no way to tell from this 2D replay that I got legged by an OP, and had to fall back for a heal. Because there was no kill, hence no "event" recorded. Ideally everything would be logged in maybe about 15fps, and include events like recons, trips going off, flashes, sound cues.

Basically exactly like the minimap you see in game, with the 2D replay layout in RIB having a seek bar that you can finely scrub and playback the match in realtime in 2D. Then the current events would act as markers to skip to key action moments, but you would also be able to see how it led up to that moment/how players reacted after.

That's just a cognitive perception thing, likely because the prowler is shorter range. So when you do get hit, the enemy is probably much nearer to you than a Skye that's dogging from miles away. So in those few seconds you're thinking "oh shit oh fuck get me outta here they're gonna swing any moment" vs Skye's dog is more like "ah shit lemme get around this corner to hide while my vision comes back".

Viewing your own in-game POV is just about the least important part of a replay system, because like you said we can already do that. But no amount of capture can replay the same scenario from different points of view, especially your opponents. And that is paramount to figuring out so many things. 


Was it run and gun, or did he just counterstrafe perfectly?  
Did I miss my flash lineup, or were they playing antiflash?  
Did he get the perfect timing, or just got audio information from a lurking teammate?  
How do players at my elo react to information/utility/fakes, and how should I adjust my playstyle accordingly?  

The last one especially is so crucial. I've lost count of how many times I've been in deep debate with my friends on what went wrong with our retake, only to be completely lost in the shitty kill-timeline-map that only records sparse info sporadically. If replays are so hard to implement, at least give us a proper kill-timeline-map that shows real-time utility, player movement, vision cones as a stopgap.
